topics.title: DBMS
topics.content_html:
Definition

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database.

Advantages over File-Processing
  • Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere.
  • Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files.
  • Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0).
  • Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization.
  • Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies.

topics.title: Data redundancy and data inconsistency
topics.content_html:
Definitions
  • Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files).
  • Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department).
DBMS Solution

A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented.

topics.title: Give the difference between a database system and a file-based system
topics.content_html:
Differences
  • Structure: DB systems store data in structured formats (tables/graphs); File systems store data in plain text/binary files.
  • Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats.
  • Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data.

topics.title: Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS
topics.content_html:
The Three Levels
  1. External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest).
  2. Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs.
  3. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations).
Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence.

topics.title: Data abstraction
topics.content_html:
Definition

Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data.

Three Levels
  • Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk.
  • Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here.
  • View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances).

topics.title: Terms schema and instance
topics.content_html:
Definition
  • Schema: The overall logical design/blueprint of the database. It changes rarely.
  • Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently.
Importance

This distinction is crucial for maintaining data independence—altering the schema (like adding a column) should not arbitrarily destroy the existing instances.

topics.title: Data independence
topics.content_html:
Definition

Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level.

Types
  • Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change.
  • Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application.

topics.title: Who are the different types of database users
topics.content_html:
Types of Users
  • Parametric (Naive) Users: End-users who interact via standard GUI applications without knowing SQL (e.g., Bank Tellers).
  • Application Programmers: Software engineers who write the backend logic connecting to the DB.
  • Sophisticated Users: Analysts who interact directly with the DB using SQL queries to generate reports.
  • Database Administrators (DBA): IT professionals who manage security, schemas, and performance tuning.

topics.title: List the responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA)
topics.content_html:
Responsibilities
  • Schema definition and modification.
  • Defining storage structures and access methods (indexing).
  • Granting user authority and managing access security.
  • Routine maintenance, database backups, and performance monitoring.

topics.title: Hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models
topics.content_html:
Comparison
  • Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers.
  • Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain.
  • Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound.
  • Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM).
Most Widely Used

The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence.

topics.title: Advantages of the relational model over the other data models
topics.content_html:
Advantages
  • Simplicity: Uses a simple tabular structure (rows and columns) that is easy to understand compared to complex graph/tree pointers.
  • Flexibility: Supports ad-hoc querying using standard SQL.
  • Data Independence: Strong separation between logical representation and physical storage.

topics.title: Terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key
topics.content_html:
Explanation
  • Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name)
  • Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email)
  • Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID)
  • Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table)

topics.title: Integrity constraints in a relational model
topics.content_html:
Definition

Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid.

The Four Constraints
  • Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer).
  • Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row.
  • Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row.
  • Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID).

topics.title: E-R model
topics.content_html:
Definition

The Entity-Relationship (E-R) model is a high-level conceptual data model that visually represents entities (objects) and the relationships between them.

Notations
  • Rectangle: Entity sets
  • Ellipse: Attributes
  • Diamond: Relationship sets
  • Lines: Link attributes to entities and entities to relationships

topics.title: Entity, entity set, attribute and relationship, and illustrate each
topics.content_html:
Definitions
  • Entity: A real-world object with independent existence (e.g., a specific student).
  • Entity Set: A collection of similar entities (e.g., all Students).
  • Attribute: A property describing an entity (e.g., Name, Age).
  • Relationship: An association among two or more entities (e.g., Student Enroll Course).

topics.title: Different types of attributes, simple, composite, derived, multivalued and key attribute,
topics.content_html:
Attribute Types
  • Simple: Indivisible atomic values (e.g., Gender).
  • Composite: Can be broken down into sub-parts (e.g., Name into First Name, Last Name).
  • Derived: Calculated from other attributes; not physically stored (e.g., Age derived from DOB).
  • Multivalued: Can hold multiple values for a single entity (e.g., Phone_Numbers).
  • Key: Uniquely identifies the entity (e.g., Roll_No).

topics.title: Different types of relationships that can exist between two entities
topics.content_html:
Cardinality Ratios
  • One-to-One (1:1): One entity in A is associated with at most one in B. (e.g., Department 1:1 Manager).
  • One-to-Many (1:N): One entity in A is associated with many in B. (e.g., Department 1:N Employees).
  • Many-to-Many (M:N): Many entities in A associated with many in B. (e.g., Student M:N Course).

topics.title: Weak entity set
topics.content_html:
Definition

A weak entity set lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key. It depends on a strong entity (identifying owner) and uses the owner's key plus its own partial key to identify rows.

Example

A Dependent (spouse/child) of an Employee. The dependent is identified by combining their Name (partial key) with the owner's Employee ID.

topics.title: Unary, binary and ternary relationships
topics.content_html:
Degrees of Relationships
  • Unary (Degree 1): Relationship between instances of a single entity set (e.g., Employee Manages Employee).
  • Binary (Degree 2): Relationship between two entity sets (e.g., Student Takes Course).
  • Ternary (Degree 3): Relationship connecting three entity sets simultaneously (e.g., Supplier Supplies Part To Project).
Exam Tip: A ternary relationship is not just three binary relationships; it represents a single fact involving all three entities together.

topics.title: Total participation and partial participation constraints in an E-R diagram
topics.content_html:
Differentiation
  • Total Participation (Mandatory): Every entity MUST participate in at least one relationship. Indicated by a double line. (e.g., Every Employee must belong to a Department).
  • Partial Participation (Optional): Only some entities may participate. Indicated by a single line. (e.g., Only some Employees are Managers of a Department).

topics.title: Generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model
topics.content_html:
Specialization (Top-Down)

The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others.
Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer, Manager, and Technician subclasses based on job role.

Generalization (Bottom-Up)

The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass.
Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass.

topics.title: Overlapping and disjoint specialization
topics.content_html:
Disjoint Specialization

An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle.
Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee, but never both at the same time.

Overlapping Specialization

An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle.
Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university.

topics.title: Aggregation in E-R modelling
topics.content_html:
Definition

Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set.

When is it required?

The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity.

Example

Consider Employee working on a Project. This forms the relationship Works_On. If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager.

topics.title: Mapping cardinality
topics.content_html:
Definition

Mapping cardinality (or cardinality ratio) expresses the number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set.

Types
  • One-to-One (1:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and vice versa.
  • One-to-Many (1:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B. An entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A.
  • Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A.
  • Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa.

topics.title: Functional dependency
topics.content_html:
Definition

A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B.

Importance

Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization. They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies.

topics.title: Insertion, deletion and update anomalies
topics.content_html:
The Three Anomalies
  • Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location).
  • Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key).
  • Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information).
How Normalization Helps

Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.

topics.title: Normalization
topics.content_html:
Definition

Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies.

The Normal Forms
  • First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell.
  • Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies).
  • Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z).

topics.title: BCNF
topics.content_html:
Definition

Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF.

Difference from 3NF

3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys.

Example

Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor). Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course.
It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key.

topics.title: Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF,
topics.content_html:
Fourth Normal Form (4NF)

Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD). A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third).
Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent).

Fifth Normal Form (5NF)

Deals with Join Dependencies. Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys.

topics.title: Lossless-join decomposition
topics.content_html:
Definition

Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data).

Condition

The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2).

Example

Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept, is a primary key for the Department table.

topics.title: Dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example
topics.content_html:
Definition

A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together.

Example

Original Relation: R(A, B, C)
Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C
Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C).
FDs in R1: A → B.
FDs in R2: B → C.
Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition.

topics.title: Consider an unnormalized relation Student_Marks(Rollno, Name, Subject, Marks) where a student appears in multiple rows, one per subject
topics.content_html:
Functional Dependencies (FDs)

Assumed FDs based on logic:

  1. FD1: Rollno → Name (A student has one name)
  2. FD2: Rollno, Subject → Marks (A specific student's marks in a specific subject)

The primary key for the unnormalized relation is (Rollno, Subject).

Step 1: 1NF to 2NF

In the original relation, Name depends ONLY on Rollno, which is a part of the primary key. This is a Partial Dependency. We decompose to eliminate it:

  • Student(Rollno, Name)
  • Performance(Rollno, Subject, Marks)
Step 2: 2NF to 3NF

In the new tables, there are no non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes (no transitive dependencies). Therefore, the tables are already in 3NF.

topics.title: Hostel management register stores the occupants of each room as shown in the table below
topics.content_html:
Problem Context

In the unnormalized table, a single cell (like "Occupants") contains multiple values (e.g., "Alice, Bob"), which violates the atomicity rule of 1NF.

1NF Solution

To convert to 1NF, we eliminate repeating groups by ensuring each cell holds only a single, atomic value. We duplicate the room number for each occupant.

Room_No Occupant
101 Alice
101 Bob
102 Charlie

Now, the primary key becomes the composite key (Room_No, Occupant).

topics.title: Table below has the composite key (StudentID, SubjectID)
topics.content_html:
Identifying Partial Dependencies

Suppose the relation is R(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Grade). The primary key is (StudentID, SubjectID).

  • StudentID → StudentName (StudentName depends only on part of the key) — Partial Dependency
  • StudentID, SubjectID → Grade (Grade depends on the whole key) — Full Dependency
Decomposition into 2NF

We split the table to remove the partial dependency:

  1. Student(StudentID, StudentName)
  2. Enrollment(StudentID, SubjectID, Grade)

Both tables are now in 2NF as all non-prime attributes fully depend on their respective primary keys.

topics.title: Table below has EmployeeID as its primary key
topics.content_html:
Violation of 3NF

Consider Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID is the primary key.

Functional Dependencies:
1. EmpID → DeptID
2. DeptID → DeptName
Because EmpID → DeptName through DeptID, this is a Transitive Dependency. 3NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on other non-prime attributes.

Decomposition into 3NF

We decompose the relation to separate the department details:

  1. Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID)
  2. Department(DeptID, DeptName)

topics.title: In the table below, each mentor teaches only one subject
topics.content_html:
Checking BCNF

Relation: R(StudentID, Subject, Mentor)
FDs: {StudentID, Subject} → Mentor, and Mentor → Subject (each mentor teaches one subject).
Because Mentor → Subject exists, but Mentor is not a super key, the table violates BCNF (even though it is in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute).

BCNF Decomposition

We must pull the violating determinant out into its own table:

  1. Mentor_Subject(Mentor, Subject)
  2. Student_Mentor(StudentID, Mentor)

Now all determinants are candidate keys.

topics.title: Table below stores a student's hobbies and the languages they know together, forcing every combination to be listed
topics.content_html:
Violation of 4NF

Relation: R(StudentID, Hobby, Language)
A student's hobbies are completely independent of the languages they speak. This creates two Multi-Valued Dependencies (MVDs):
StudentID ⟶ Hobby and StudentID ⟶ Language.
Storing them together forces a Cartesian product (e.g., 2 hobbies × 3 languages = 6 rows for one student). Since 4NF forbids non-trivial MVDs, this violates 4NF.

4NF Decomposition

Split into two tables to eliminate the Cartesian product:

  1. Student_Hobby(StudentID, Hobby)
  2. Student_Language(StudentID, Language)

topics.title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E)
topics.content_html:
Computing {A, C}+
  1. Start with the base set: {A, C}
  2. Using A → B, add B. The set becomes {A, B, C}
  3. Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D}
  4. Using D → E, add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E}
Conclusion

Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key. Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key.

topics.title: Consider the relation Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Course_Name, Instructor)
topics.content_html:
Analysis

Primary Key: (Roll_No, Course_ID)
The FD Course_ID → Course_Name is a Partial Dependency because Course_Name depends only on a part of the primary key (Course_ID), violating 2NF.

2NF Decomposition
  1. Course(Course_ID, Course_Name)
  2. Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Instructor)

Now, both relations are in 2NF.

topics.title: Consider the relation Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location)
topics.content_html:
Analysis

Primary Key: Emp_ID. Since the key is a single attribute, there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF.
However, the FD Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location creates a Transitive Dependency (Emp_ID → Dept_ID → Dept_Name). This violates 3NF.

3NF Decomposition
  1. Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID)
  2. Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location)

topics.title: Consider the relation R(Student, Subject, Teacher)
topics.content_html:
Analysis

Candidate Keys: (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher).
For the FD Teacher → Subject, Teacher is a determinant but not a super key. Therefore, R violates BCNF.

BCNF Decomposition
  1. Teach_Subj(Teacher, Subject)
  2. Stud_Teach(Student, Teacher)

Both tables are now strictly in BCNF.

topics.title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D)
topics.content_html:
Candidate Keys
  • {A, B}+ = {A, B, C, D}
  • {B, C}+ = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A)
  • {B, D}+ = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C)

The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD. All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key).

Highest Normal Form

Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF.
However, check BCNF: The FD C → D has determinant C, which is not a super key. Thus, it violates BCNF. The highest normal form is 3NF.

topics.title: RDBMS
topics.content_html:
Feature DBMS RDBMS
Data Storage Stores data as files. Stores data in tabular form (rows and columns).
Relationships Does not support relationships easily. Supports complex relationships using foreign keys.

topics.title: Entities and relationships of the E-R model are represented in a relational database
topics.content_html:
• Strong Entities: Represented as standalone tables.
  • Relationships (1:N): The primary key of the '1' side is added as a foreign key to the 'N' side table.
  • Relationships (M:N): Handled by creating a new junction table containing the primary keys of both entities.

topics.content_html:
i. Names of students enrolled in 'DBMS'

πsname ( σcname='DBMS' (Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Course) )

ii. Courses where 'Alice' is enrolled

πcname ( σsname='Alice' (Course ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Student) )

topics.title: Derived operations of relational algebra
topics.content_html:
Derived operations are built using fundamental operations (σ, π, ×, ∪, -).

  • Intersection (∩): Returns tuples existing in both relations.
  • Join (⨝): A cartesian product followed by a selection.
  • Division (÷): Used for queries involving the word "every" (e.g., students who took all courses).

topics.title: Relational algebra and relational calculus
topics.content_html:
Relational Algebra Relational Calculus
Procedural query language. Non-procedural (declarative) query language.
Specifies what data is required and how to retrieve it. Specifies what data is required without specifying how to retrieve it.

topics.title: Degree and cardinality of a relation
topics.content_html:
• Degree: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation.
  • Cardinality: The number of tuples (rows) in a relation.

topics.title: Domain relational calculus
topics.content_html:
Domain Relational Calculus (DRC) is a declarative query language where variables represent single attribute values (domains).

Syntax: { <x1, x2, ..., xn> | P(x1, x2, ..., xn) }

Example: { <N> | ∃ I, A, C ( <I, N, A, C> ∈ Student ∧ A > 20 ) }

topics.title: DDL, DML, DCL and TCL commands
topics.content_html:
• DDL: Defines structure (e.g., CREATE TABLE).
  • DML: Manages data (e.g., INSERT INTO).
  • DCL: Manages security (e.g., GRANT).
  • TCL: Manages transactions (e.g., COMMIT).

topics.title: Use of CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE commands
topics.content_html:
• CREATE: Used to create new tables/objects.
  • ALTER: Used to modify an existing table structure (add/drop columns).
  • DROP: Deletes an entire table and its structure.
  • TRUNCATE: Deletes all rows rapidly, but keeps the structure intact.

topics.title: DML commands INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT
topics.content_html:
• INSERT: Adds new rows.
  • UPDATE: Modifies existing rows.
  • DELETE: Removes specific rows.
  • SELECT: Retrieves data from the database.

topics.title: Purpose of GRANT and REVOKE commands in SQL
topics.content_html:
GRANT and REVOKE belong to the DCL (Data Control Language) category. They are used to manage database security by controlling user privileges.

  • GRANT: Gives a user or role specific privileges on database objects.
    Example: GRANT SELECT ON Employees TO user_alice;
  • REVOKE: Removes previously granted privileges.
    Example: REVOKE SELECT ON Employees FROM user_alice;

topics.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT
topics.content_html:
These are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands used to manage transactions.

  • COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made during the current transaction.
  • ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made in the current transaction.
  • SAVEPOINT: Creates a checkpoint within a transaction to rollback to later.
BEGIN;
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1;
SAVEPOINT SP1;
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2;
ROLLBACK TO SP1; -- Undoes the second update
COMMIT; -- Permanently saves the first update

topics.title: Join
topics.content_html:
A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column.

Inner Join

Returns only rows with matching values in both tables.

SELECT A.Name, B.Dept FROM Emp A INNER JOIN Dept B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID;
Outer Joins
  • Left Outer: Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right.
  • Right Outer: Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left.
  • Full Outer: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table.

topics.title: Equi join and a natural join,
topics.content_html:
Equi Join Natural Join
Explicitly uses the equality operator (=) in the ON clause. Implicitly matches on all columns that have the same name. No ON clause is used.
Output contains duplicate matching columns. Output automatically removes duplicate matching columns.
SELECT * FROM Emp JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.DeptID; SELECT * FROM Emp NATURAL JOIN Dept;

topics.title: Self join
topics.content_html:
Self Join

A table is joined with itself using aliases.

SELECT E.Name AS Employee, M.Name AS Manager 
FROM Employee E 
JOIN Employee M ON E.ManagerID = M.EmpID;
Cross Join

Produces the Cartesian Product of two tables (every row matched with every row).

SELECT T.Name, C.RoomNo FROM Teachers T CROSS JOIN Classrooms C;

topics.title: Aggregate functions available in SQL, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN, giving an example of each
topics.content_html:
Aggregate functions perform a calculation on a set of values and return a single summarizing value.

  • COUNT(): Returns the number of rows. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees;
  • SUM(): Returns the total sum of a column. SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM Employees;
  • AVG(): Returns the average value. SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees;
  • MAX() / MIN(): Returns the largest / smallest value. SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees;

topics.title: Purpose of the GROUP BY clause
topics.content_html:
The GROUP BY clause is used to arrange identical data into groups. It is typically used in conjunction with aggregate functions (COUNT, MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG).

Scenario: Find the total number of employees in each department.

SELECT DeptID, COUNT(EmpID) AS TotalEmployees
FROM Employee
GROUP BY DeptID;

topics.title: How is the HAVING clause different from the WHERE clause
topics.content_html:
WHERE Clause HAVING Clause
Filters individual rows before grouping. Filters groups after grouping.
Cannot contain aggregate functions. Can contain aggregate functions.
Example
SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee
WHERE HireDate > '2020-01-01'  -- Filters rows first
GROUP BY DeptID
HAVING AVG(Salary) > 50000;    -- Filters groups

topics.title: Use of the ORDER BY clause
topics.content_html:
The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set of a query in either ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.

Example: SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC;

topics.title: Nested queries
topics.content_html:
A nested query (subquery) is a query embedded within another query. They are used to break down complex queries into isolated steps.

Scenario: Find employees who earn a salary greater than the average salary.

SELECT Name, Salary 
FROM Employee 
WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);

topics.title: Correlated subquery
topics.content_html:
Simple Subquery Correlated Subquery
Executes completely independent of the outer query. Depends on the outer query for its values.
Executes exactly once for the entire outer query. Executes repeatedly, once for every row processed by the outer query.
Example (Correlated)
SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee E1 
WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee E2 WHERE E1.DeptID = E2.DeptID);

topics.title: Use of IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL operators in a nested query
topics.content_html:
• IN: Checks if a value matches any value in a list or subquery result.
    WHERE DeptID IN (SELECT DeptID FROM Departments)
  • EXISTS: Evaluates to TRUE if the subquery returns one or more records.
    WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustID = Customers.ID)
  • ANY (or SOME): Compares a value to each value in a list and evaluates to TRUE if any comparison is true.
    WHERE Salary > ANY (SELECT Salary FROM IT_Dept)
  • ALL: Evaluates to TRUE only if the comparison is true for all values in the list.
    WHERE Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM Interns)

topics.title: View
topics.content_html:
A View is a virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement. It contains rows and columns, just like a real table, but holds no data of its own.

Advantages
  • Security: Restricts access to specific rows/columns of a table.
  • Simplicity: Hides complex joins and calculations into a single virtual table.
  • Data Independence: Insulates applications from changes in base table structures.

topics.title: Simple view and a materialized view
topics.content_html:
Simple View Materialized View
Virtual table; does not store data physically. Stores the actual result data physically on disk.
Query is executed every time the view is accessed. Data is pre-computed, providing much faster read access.
Always shows up-to-date real-time data. Needs to be refreshed periodically to show updated data.

topics.title: Can every view be updated
topics.content_html:
No, not all views can be updated. A view is updatable only if the DBMS can unambiguously trace the update back to the underlying base table rows.

Limitations (Cannot Update If:)
  • It contains aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX).
  • It contains GROUP BY or HAVING clauses.
  • It is built using multiple tables (Joins), depending on the DBMS.
  • It uses the DISTINCT keyword.
Example

A view CREATE VIEW Dept_Salaries AS SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID; cannot be updated because an update to an average salary cannot be mapped to individual employees.

topics.title: Generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model
topics.content_html:
Specialization (Top-Down)

The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics.
Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp.

Generalization (Bottom-Up)

The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass.
Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle.

Aggregation

Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships.
Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity.

topics.title: Decomposition
topics.content_html:
Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

Lossless-Join Decomposition

A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples.

Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2).

Dependency-Preserving Decomposition

A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together.

topics.title: How is decomposition related to normalization
topics.content_html:
Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form.

Example

Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName.

  • This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency (EmpID → DeptID → DeptName).
  • Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy:
    1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID)
    2. Department(DeptID, DeptName)

This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving.

topics.title: Relational algebra
topics.content_html:
Feature Relational Algebra SQL
Nature Theoretical, mathematical foundation. Procedural. Practical, commercial language. Declarative.
Selection (Rows) σcondition(Table) WHERE condition
Projection (Columns) πcol1, col2(Table) SELECT col1, col2
Joins Table1 ⨝ Table2 Table1 JOIN Table2
Duplicates Automatically removes duplicates (set semantics). Retains duplicates by default (bag semantics); requires DISTINCT to remove.

topics.title: Write a query to display the names of students who are enrolled in the course 'DBMS'
topics.content_html:
Assuming the standard schema: Student(sid, sname), Course(cid, cname), Enrollment(sid, cid).

SELECT s.sname 
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid
WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS';
Alternative (Using Subqueries)
SELECT sname FROM Student 
WHERE sid IN (
    SELECT sid FROM Enrollment 
    WHERE cid IN (
        SELECT cid FROM Course WHERE cname = 'DBMS'
    )
);

topics.title: Write a query to display, course-wise, how many students have enrolled in each course
topics.content_html:
Using the standard schema: Course(cid, cname), Enrollment(sid, cid).

SELECT c.cname, COUNT(e.sid) AS NumberOfStudents
FROM Course c
JOIN Enrollment e ON c.cid = e.cid
GROUP BY c.cid, c.cname;

topics.title: Write a query
topics.content_html:
SELECT s.sname, COUNT(e.cid) AS EnrolledCourses
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
GROUP BY s.sid, s.sname
HAVING COUNT(e.cid) > 3;

topics.title: Write a query to display the student name along
topics.content_html:
We use a standard INNER JOIN to connect the three tables.

SELECT s.sname, c.cname
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid;

topics.title: Write a query to find students who have not enrolled in any course so far
topics.content_html:
Using LEFT JOIN
SELECT s.sname 
FROM Student s
LEFT JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
WHERE e.cid IS NULL;
Using NOT EXISTS 
SELECT sname FROM Student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid
);

topics.title: Write a nested query to find the student(s) who scored the highest marks in the course 'DBMS'
topics.content_html:
Assuming Enrollment(sid, cid, marks).

SELECT s.sname, e.marks
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid
WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS' 
  AND e.marks = (
      SELECT MAX(e2.marks) 
      FROM Enrollment e2
      JOIN Course c2 ON e2.cid = c2.cid
      WHERE c2.cname = 'DBMS'
  );

topics.title: Create a view that shows the student name, course name and marks for every enrollment record
topics.content_html:
CREATE VIEW Student_Grades AS
SELECT s.sname, c.cname, e.marks
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid
JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid;

You can then query this view like a regular table: SELECT * FROM Student_Grades;

topics.title: Write a relational algebra expression to retrieve the names of students enrolled in the course 'DBMS'
topics.content_html:
Relational Algebra:

πsname ( Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ σcname='DBMS'(Course) )

Breakdown:

  1. Select only the course where cname is 'DBMS' (σ).
  2. Natural Join (⨝) the result with Enrollment and Student.
  3. Project (π) only the student name (sname).

topics.title: Using the division operation of relational algebra, write an expression to find students who are enrolled in every course offered
topics.content_html:
The division operator (÷) is used specifically for queries involving "every" or "all".

Expression:

πsid(Enrollment) ÷ πcid(Course)

To get the student names, we natural join this result with the Student table:

πsname ( Student ⨝ (πsid, cid(Enrollment) ÷ πcid(Course)) )

topics.title: Write a correlated subquery to list students who have scored more than the average marks obtained in their respective course
topics.content_html:
SELECT s.sname, e1.cid, e1.marks
FROM Student s
JOIN Enrollment e1 ON s.sid = e1.sid
WHERE e1.marks > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.marks)
    FROM Enrollment e2
    WHERE e1.cid = e2.cid
);

The inner query recalculates the average marks dynamically for every row of the outer query, matching the cid.

topics.title: Use of CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE commands
topics.content_html:
CREATE TABLE is used to create a new table in the database.

ALTER TABLE is used to add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table.

DROP TABLE is used to delete an existing table completely (including its structure and data).

DDL statements are auto-committed because they alter the database schema directly and cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS like MySQL and Oracle.

topics.title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a Library_Book table having Book_ID, Title, Author, Price and Published_Date, choosing appropriate data types
topics.content_html:
CREATE TABLE Library_Book (
    Book_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Title VARCHAR(100),
    Author VARCHAR(50),
    Price DECIMAL(8,2),
    Published_Date DATE
);

topics.title: Write a query to add a column Email of type VARCHAR(40) to the Student table
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Student
ADD Email VARCHAR(40);

topics.title: Write a query to change the data type of the Fees column in the Student table to DECIMAL(10,2)
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Student
MODIFY Fees DECIMAL(10,2);

topics.title: Write a query to rename the Course column of the Student table as Program
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Student
RENAME COLUMN Course TO Program;

(Note: Syntax varies slightly between RDBMS. In older MySQL versions, CHANGE Course Program VARCHAR(...) is used).

topics.title: Write a query to rename the table Student to Student_Info
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Student
RENAME TO Student_Info;

Alternatively: RENAME TABLE Student TO Student_Info;

topics.title: Using CREATE TABLE
topics.content_html:
CREATE TABLE Student_Backup AS
SELECT * FROM Student;

topics.title: Give the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP commands
topics.content_html:
• DELETE is a DML command used to remove specific rows based on a WHERE clause. It can be rolled back.
  • TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows from a table quickly by deallocating the pages. It cannot be rolled back and resets identity columns.
  • DROP is a DDL command that completely deletes the table structure and its data from the database.

topics.title: Five constraints NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK, giving an example of each
topics.content_html:
NOT NULL: Ensures a column cannot have a NULL value. Ex: Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL

UNIQUE: Ensures all values in a column are distinct. Ex: Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE

PRIMARY KEY: Uniquely identifies each record. It is NOT NULL + UNIQUE. Ex: ID INT PRIMARY KEY

FOREIGN KEY: Ensures referential integrity by linking to a primary key in another table. Ex: FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES Dept(ID)

CHECK: Ensures values in a column satisfy a specific condition. Ex: Age INT CHECK (Age >= 18)

topics.title: Column-level and a table-level constraint
topics.content_html:
Column-level constraints are defined immediately after the data type of a column. Table-level constraints are defined at the end of the table creation and can span multiple columns.

A table-level constraint is compulsory when defining a composite key (a constraint that involves more than one column).

topics.title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), keeping Dept_ID as the primary key
topics.content_html:
CREATE TABLE Department (
    Dept_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Dept_Name VARCHAR(50)
);

topics.title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Dept_ID, Salary), where Emp_ID is the primary key, Name cannot be left blank and Email must be unique
topics.content_html:
CREATE TABLE Employee (
    Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE,
    Dept_ID INT,
    Salary DECIMAL(10,2)
);

topics.title: Using ALTER TABLE, add a foreign key on Employee
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Employee
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept
FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID);

topics.title: Using ALTER TABLE, put a check constraint on the Employee table so that Salary is always greater than zero
topics.content_html:
ALTER TABLE Employee
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0);

topics.title: Table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint but only one PRIMARY KEY
topics.content_html: A Primary Key is strictly designed to be the single, definitive row identifier used by the database engine to organize and index the physical storage (e.g. clustered index). There can only be one physical ordering. However, multiple columns may have naturally unique data (like an Email or Phone number), which is why multiple UNIQUE constraints are permitted to enforce business rules.

topics.title: Numeric functions ROUND, TRUNCATE, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT, giving an example of each
topics.content_html:
• ROUND(n, d): Rounds n to d decimal places. ROUND(3.456, 2) → 3.46
  • TRUNCATE(n, d): Cuts off n at d decimal places without rounding. TRUNCATE(3.456, 2) → 3.45
  • CEIL(n): Returns the smallest integer ≥ n. CEIL(3.14) → 4
  • FLOOR(n): Returns the largest integer ≤ n. FLOOR(3.8) → 3
  • ABS(n): Returns the absolute (positive) value. ABS(-5) → 5
  • MOD(x, y): Returns the remainder of x/y. MOD(10, 3) → 1
  • POWER(x, y): Returns x raised to power y. POWER(2, 3) → 8
  • SQRT(n): Returns the square root. SQRT(16) → 4

topics.title: Round off 78
topics.content_html:
SELECT ROUND(78.3456, 2);    -- Result: 78.35
SELECT TRUNCATE(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.34

Reason: ROUND evaluates the third decimal digit (5) and mathematically rounds up. TRUNCATE simply drops all digits after the 2nd decimal place without any mathematical evaluation.

topics.title: Write a query on PRODUCT_MAST to display each Product_Name along
topics.content_html:
SELECT Product_Name, ROUND(Price, 0) AS Rounded_Price
FROM PRODUCT_MAST;

topics.title: Find the remainder when 29 is divided by 4
topics.content_html:
-- Find remainder
SELECT MOD(29, 4);

-- Check if odd/even (if remainder is 1, it is odd)
SELECT MOD(29, 2);

topics.title: Find the square of 12
topics.content_html: SELECT POWER(12, 2) AS Square, SQRT(144) AS Root;

topics.title: Date functions CURDATE, DATEDIFF, DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB and DATE_FORMAT, giving an example of each
topics.content_html:
• CURDATE(): Returns the current system date. Ex: SELECT CURDATE();
  • DATEDIFF(date1, date2): Returns the number of days between two dates. Ex: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-10-10', '2023-10-01'); → 9
  • DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit): Adds a time interval to a date. Ex: SELECT DATE_ADD('2023-01-01', INTERVAL 5 DAY);
  • DATE_FORMAT(date, format): Formats a date string. Ex: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE(), '%Y-%m-%d');

topics.title: String functions CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTRING and TRIM/REPLACE, giving an example of each
topics.content_html:
• CONCAT(s1, s2): Joins two or more strings. Ex: CONCAT('Data', 'base') → 'Database'
  • UPPER(s) / LOWER(s): Converts a string to all uppercase or lowercase. Ex: UPPER('sql') → 'SQL'
  • LENGTH(s): Returns the number of characters in a string. Ex: LENGTH('DBMS') → 4
  • SUBSTRING(s, start, len): Extracts a part of a string. Ex: SUBSTRING('Database', 1, 4) → 'Data'
  • TRIM(s): Removes leading and trailing spaces. Ex: TRIM(' SQL ') → 'SQL'
  • REPLACE(s, old, new): Replaces all occurrences of a substring. Ex: REPLACE('DBMS', 'M', 'B') → 'DBBS'

topics.title: Using DATEDIFF, find the number of days between '2023-01-01' and '2023-12-31'
topics.content_html:
SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-12-31', '2023-01-01') AS Days_Difference;

(Note: Syntax may vary slightly by DBMS. In MySQL, it returns 364.)

topics.title: Using DATE_ADD, add 45 days to the date '2024-02-01'
topics.content_html: SELECT DATE_ADD('2024-02-01', INTERVAL 45 DAY) AS New_Date;

topics.title: Write a query to extract only the year and month from the date '2025-03-22'
topics.content_html:
SELECT YEAR('2025-03-22') AS Year, MONTH('2025-03-22') AS Month;

Alternatively, using DATE_FORMAT in MySQL: SELECT DATE_FORMAT('2025-03-22', '%Y-%m');

topics.title: Write a query on the STUDENT table that displays the full name of every student by joining First_Name and Last_Name
topics.content_html:
SELECT CONCAT(First_Name, ' ', Last_Name) AS Full_Name 
FROM STUDENT;

topics.title: Find the length of the string 'Normalization', and separately extract its first six characters
topics.content_html:
SELECT LENGTH('Normalization') AS Str_Length,
       SUBSTRING('Normalization', 1, 6) AS Extracted_Str;

topics.title: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT
topics.content_html:
Set Operators:

  • UNION: Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates.
  • UNION ALL: Combines results of two queries, keeping all duplicates.
  • INTERSECT: Returns only the rows that appear in both queries.
  • MINUS / EXCEPT: Returns rows from the first query that are not present in the second.

Condition for application (Union Compatibility):

  1. Both SELECT statements must have the same number of columns.
  2. The corresponding columns must have compatible data types in the same order.

topics.title: Write a query to list every student who is a member of CLUB_CODING or CLUB_MUSIC or both,
topics.content_html:
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING
UNION
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

topics.title: Write a query that lists all the rows of CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC together without removing duplicate names
topics.content_html:
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING
UNION ALL
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

topics.title: Write a query to find students who are members of both CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC
topics.content_html:
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING
INTERSECT
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

topics.title: Write a query to find students who are in CLUB_CODING but not in CLUB_MUSIC
topics.content_html:
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING
EXCEPT   -- (or MINUS in Oracle)
SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

Yes, the order matters. A EXCEPT B returns elements in A that are not in B. B EXCEPT A would return students in CLUB_MUSIC who are not in CLUB_CODING.

topics.title: Transaction
topics.content_html:
A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely or not at all.

ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B):

  • Atomicity: "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.
  • Consistency: The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway.
  • Durability: Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes.

Transaction State Diagram

topics.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT
topics.content_html:
• COMMIT: Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently.
  • ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit.
  • SAVEPOINT: Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101';
SAVEPOINT step1;
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102';
-- If something goes wrong here:
ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update
COMMIT; -- Saves the final state

topics.title: Write a transaction that transfers Rs
topics.content_html:
START TRANSACTION;
SAVEPOINT before_transfer;

UPDATE ACCOUNT 
SET Balance = Balance - 3000 
WHERE Acc_No = 'A102';

UPDATE ACCOUNT 
SET Balance = Balance + 3000 
WHERE Acc_No = 'A103';

COMMIT;

topics.title: Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise
topics.content_html:
SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance,
    CASE 
        WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High'
        WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS Balance_Category
FROM ACCOUNT;

topics.title: Write a query
topics.content_html:
SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance,
    IF(Balance < 15000, 'Low Balance Alert', 'OK') AS Status
FROM ACCOUNT;

topics.content_html:

topics.title: In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger
topics.content_html:
• Stored Procedure: A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine.
  • Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT): Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys.
  • Cursor: A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure.
  • Trigger: A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table.

topics.title: BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger
topics.content_html:
BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables).

NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted).

topics.title: Purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure
topics.content_html:
Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing.

  • DECLARE ... HANDLER: Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION).
  • SIGNAL: Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
